summary: Defines a CLASSTYPE object for PCEP to support Diffserv-aware traffic engineering when paths are computed with the help of a PCE. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Different kinds of traffic need different treatment, like regular and express lanes. This lets a route-planner request a route for the right class.

questions: what is the pcep classtype object
what is a class-type in ds-te
subtitle: A small PCEP object that tells a path computation element which traffic class a requested tunnel belongs to.

tldr.problem: Diffserv-aware traffic engineering enforces separate bandwidth constraints per class of traffic, but PCEP had no way to say which Class-Type a requested path belongs to.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5455 defines the CLASSTYPE object, a 3-bit Class-Type carried in a path computation request, so the PCE can pick the right bandwidth constraint when computing the path.
tldr.outcome: A PCC includes the object for Class-Types 1 to 7 and omits it for Class 0, which keeps older PCEs working. New error codes cover unsupported or invalid values.

today: RFC 5455 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 5440, which defines PCEP.

sections.title: Why PCEP Needs a Class-Type
sections.content:
RFC 5440 defines the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP), used between a Path Computation Client (PCC) and a Path Computation Element (PCE), or between two PCEs. Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE) enforces different bandwidth constraints for different classes of traffic, rather than one aggregate constraint across all classes.

RFC 4657 says PCEP must support the traffic Class-Type as an MPLS-TE-specific constraint. As defined in RFC 5440, though, a path computation request cannot carry one. This document adds a new object, CLASSTYPE, so the PCE can identify the bandwidth constraint of the TE LSP it is computing a path for.
sections.eli5: A route-planner used to hear only where you wanted to go. Now you can also tell it what kind of traffic is traveling, so it picks a route with the right rules.

sections.title: Terms: Class-Type, TE-Class and Friends
sections.content:
A Class-Type (CT) is a set of Traffic Trunks governed by a set of bandwidth constraints, used for link bandwidth allocation, constraint-based routing and admission control. A given Traffic Trunk belongs to the same CT on all links. A Traffic Trunk is an aggregation of traffic flows of the same class placed inside a TE LSP.

A TE-Class is a pair of a Class-Type and a preemption priority allowed for that Class-Type. An LSP carrying a trunk of that Class-Type can use the priority as its setup priority, holding priority, or both.
sections.eli5: A Class-Type is like a ticket colour that decides which bandwidth budget you draw from. A TE-Class is the ticket colour plus how important your ticket is.

sections.title: The CLASSTYPE Object
sections.content:
The CLASSTYPE object is optional. It has the PCEP common object header from RFC 5440 followed by one 32-bit word of body. Its object class is 22 and its object type is 1. Because the PCE must take the object into account if it is included, the P flag MUST be set. The I flag is ignored.

The body has two fields. CT is a 3-bit field holding the Class-Type; allowed values are 1 to 7, and 0 is reserved. The other 29 bits are Reserved: they MUST be zero on transmission and MUST be ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: The object is a tiny label: a short header, then one small number saying which class the traffic is in. The rest of the label is left blank on purpose.

sections.title: Placement in the Request Message
sections.content:
RFC 5440 sets the order of objects in PCEP messages. This document inserts CLASSTYPE in the Path Computation Request (PCReq) right after the END-POINTS object and before the optional LSPA, BANDWIDTH, metric, RRO, IRO and LOAD-BALANCING objects.

Implementations MUST form PCEP messages using the object ordering rules written in Backus-Naur Form.
sections.eli5: Like a form with boxes in a fixed order, the class box goes right after the start and end points.

sections.title: How Requests Are Processed
sections.content:
If the LSP belongs to Class-Type N, where N is 1 to 7, the PCC building the PCReq MUST include a CLASSTYPE object with CT set to N. If the LSP belongs to Class 0, the request MUST NOT contain the object. That keeps requests compatible with a PCE that does not know the object. When the object is absent, Class-Type 0 is assumed.

If a request holds several CLASSTYPE objects, only the first counts; the rest MUST be ignored and MUST NOT be forwarded. The object is meaningful only in requests, and a reply MUST NOT include it. A PCE that forwards a request to another PCE MUST remember the Class-Type so it can finish the computation when the reply arrives.

TE-Class is found from the CT value together with the setup priority in the LSPA object. If LSPA is absent, the setup priority is assumed to be 0. The RFC adds that a PCE and PCC should share an understanding of Class-Types and TE-Classes, with global significance if a request crosses an Autonomous System boundary; enforcing that is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Ordinary traffic needs no special label. Anything special gets one class label, and if someone stuck on several, only the first is read.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
A PCE that does not recognize the object MUST reject the whole PCEP message and send an error with Error-Type "Unknown Object" or "Not supported object" from RFC 5440. A PCE that recognizes it but sees the P flag clear MUST send the error defined in RFC 5440.

This document defines Error-Type 12, Diffserv-aware TE error, with three values:

  • 1: Unsupported Class-Type, for a Class-Type the PCE does not support.
  • 2: Invalid Class-Type, for example a CT value of 0.
  • 3: Class-Type and setup priority do not form a configured TE-class.
sections.eli5: If the planner does not know the class, or the class is not allowed, it sends back a note saying exactly which problem it hit.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC says it does not introduce new security issues, and the security considerations of PCEP in RFC 5440 remain relevant.

IANA allocated object class 22, named CLASSTYPE, with object type 1 (Class-Type), in the PCEP object registry. It also allocated Error-Type 12 with error values 1, 2 and 3 as listed above.
sections.eli5: Adding one small label does not open any new doors for trouble, so the old safety rules still cover it.

fields.name: PCEP common header
fields.desc: Common object header from RFC 5440; object class 22, object type 1, P flag set.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: CT
fields.desc: Class-Type; values 1 to 7 are allowed and 0 is reserved.

items.label: Unsupported Class-Type
items.desc: The PCE recognizes the object but does not support this Class-Type.

items.label: Invalid Class-Type
items.desc: The Class-Type value is not valid, for example 0.

items.label: No configured TE-class
items.desc: Class-Type and setup priority do not form a configured TE-class.
